scenario: AITA for no longer cooking for my roommate because he dumps condiments on everything? | Because I love cooking and (at the risk of sounding arrogant) I'm pretty good at it, I've always volunteered to be in charge of dinner when dividing up chores with roommates. I'm **not** saying my food is perfect. There are a lot of things I'm trying to improve on. But I learned to cook from two professional chefs, I don't have a lot of typical issues like under-seasoning or over-cooking food, and even when I'm living with other people that are also good at cooking I'm usually asked to prepare food 3+ nights a week. Even if I'm not incredible, I at least know what I'm doing. Since this comes up later: we have a shared food budget for staples/basic ingredients (pasta, broth, canned vegetables, flour, sugar, spices, etc). Half the time we'll split the cost of meat and fresh ingredients, half the time I pay for them myself and and accept booze, snacks (another roommate is a phenomenal baker), chores, or favors as payment. The problem is, one of my newer roommates puts condiments on everything he eats. I'm not just talking about things like hamburgers, chicken wings, mac and cheese, or anything else that normally gets condiments. I've seen him put ketchup, mayo, hot sauce, A1, or barbeque sauce on chili, steak, alfredo, fried rice, curry, pizza, red sauce, gumbo, ribs that are already covered in BBQ sauce... you get the idea. And that would be fine, I guess, but he A) does it without even trying the food first and B) completely smothers the food with them. I've tried to talk to him about this. I offered to make his favorite meals, but even stuff he says he likes prepared the way he says he likes it gets the same treatment. I've asked him to at least try the food first but he refuses. I've explained that it bothers me when I put effort into a meal and he treats it the same way he treats fast food and microwave dinners, but he said it was still being eaten so it didn't matter. I finally got frustrated and told him not to give me anything for fresh ingredients anymore because I was done cooking for him. He's been complaining to my other two roommates because his monthly expenses have gone way up (he doesn't cook at all, so he either eats out or buys prepackage meals) and saying that I'm being petty and over dramatic. My baking roommate says she agrees with my decision and the other roommate doesn't care, he just wants mealtimes to be less dramatic. AITA? I think I did plenty to meet him halfway.

message.reasoning:
Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether the action in this scenario is morally acceptable or not. Let me read through the scenario again to make sure I understand it properly.

The person is a man who has been cooking for his roommates because he enjoys it and is good at it. He's been handling dinner chores, and even though he's not perfect, he's usually asked to cook several nights a week. They have a shared food budget for staples, and sometimes he covers the cost of meat and fresh ingredients, expecting payment in other forms like booze, snacks, or chores.

The problem arises with one of his newer roommates who puts condiments on everything, regardless of the dish. He doesn't try the food first and completely smothers it with condiments. The roommate doesn't care that it bothers the cook, saying it's still being eaten. The cook tried talking to him, offering to make his favorite meals, but the roommate still adds condiments. The cook got frustrated and told the roommate not to contribute to fresh ingredients anymore, effectively stopping cooking for him. Now the roommate is complaining to others, saying the cook is being petty.

The question is whether the cook's action is morally acceptable.

First, I need to consider the moral principles involved here. The cook is upset because his roommate is ruining the meals he puts effort into. The roommate's behavior is disrespectful to the cook's efforts. The cook tried to communicate and find a solution but was unsuccessful. He then decided to stop cooking for the roommate, which affected the roommate's expenses since he doesn't cook and now has to eat out or buy prepackaged meals.

On one hand, the cook is entitled to his feelings and should feel respected for his efforts. It's reasonable to expect that his roommate would at least try the food before adding condiments. The roommate's refusal to do so and his dismissive attitude could be seen as disrespectful. The cook tried to address the issue, so he's not just acting out of frustration without trying to resolve it.

On the other hand, the cook's decision to stop cooking for the roommate might be seen as a bit harsh. However, considering that he had already made efforts to accommodate the roommate and the roommate was unresponsive, it might be justified. The cook is also not refusing to cook at all; he's just not cooking for this particular roommate anymore, which seems like a proportional response.

Additionally, the roommate's complaint about increased expenses might be a result of his own choices. He doesn't cook, so he has to rely on others or spend more on prepackaged meals. The cook's action is a consequence of the roommate's behavior, not an unreasonable demand.

I think the cook's action is morally acceptable because he had tried to resolve the issue, communicated his feelings, and the roommate was uncooperative. The cook's decision to stop cooking for him is a reasonable response to the disrespect and lack of consideration from the roommate.
